title: The moon
hook: some sight the moon locally, some follow another country, some use calculation

segments.voice: Yesterday, touching and wudu, and your line: details differ. Did a small rule surprise you, and did you find the reading behind it? Day one thousand two hundred ten.

Eid morning, and the group chat is arguing. One cousin is already in new clothes, posting photos from the mosque. Another is still fasting, because her mosque says the month has one more day. A third says his community decided weeks ago, by the numbers. Same city, same family, same Ramadan, and two different Eids. It comes from one question about a crescent, answered more than one way. Today, the moon.
screen: `EID MORNING, THE CHAT IS ARGUING.` → `ONE COUSIN FEASTS, ONE FASTS.` → `ONE QUESTION, SEVERAL ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: First, why the moon at all. The Islamic months follow the moon, and the Qur'an says of the new moons, in Pickthall's words, "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage." A month begins with the thin crescent, the hilal, just after sunset. Next, the instruction. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says: fast when you see it, and stop fasting when you see it, and if it's hidden from you, complete the month as thirty days. Seeing is at the heart of it. Then, the first question: whose seeing? In Sahih Muslim, Kurayb travels from Syria to Medina. In Syria, he says, people saw the new moon on Friday night and began fasting. Ibn Abbas, in Medina, answers that they saw it on Saturday night, and they'll keep counting by their own sighting. This is how we were told, he says. Some scholars read that as each region sighting its own moon. Others say one sighting anywhere should bind everyone who hears of it, and so some communities follow the announcement of another country. Last, the second question: what counts as seeing? Some jurists say an eye on the horizon, nothing else. Others answer that astronomers can now say ahead of time when the crescent will be born and when it can be seen, and that a reliable calculation can stand in for the eye, or at least rule out a mistaken sighting. Some councils announce the dates far in advance. So the family chat is arguing over three readings of one sentence about a crescent.
screen: `THE MONTHS FOLLOW THE MOON.` · `FAST WHEN YOU SEE IT.` · `KURAYB, IBN ABBAS: WHOSE SEEING?` · `THE EYE, OR THE CALCULATION?`

segments.voice: The practice: learn your mosque's method, and look at the sky. If you have a mosque, make a note to ask how it decides the start of the month: local sighting, another country's announcement, or calculation. Then tonight, if you can, step outside and find the moon, or the place it would be. For now, picture it: the thin silver edge low in the west after sunset, the way it looks to anyone waiting for it. Breathe slowly while you hold it. The bell holds the time.
The moon. The new crescent begins each Islamic month; some sight it locally, some follow another country's sighting, some use calculation. Today's word.

Your line: which moon? Today, find out when your local calendar says the next month begins, and how it decided. Tomorrow, the odd prayer of the night, prayed in many ways. Day one thousand two hundred ten.

howItsDone: Mosques and councils start the Islamic months, including Ramadan and the Eids, by one of several methods: a local sighting of the crescent, following another country's announced sighting, or astronomical calculation.

fork.setup: you're Ibn Abbas in Medina. Kurayb arrives: Syria saw the new moon a night before you did. do you change your count?
options: no, keep counting by Medina's own sighting.
fork.reveal: Ibn Abbas keeps Medina's sighting and says, this is how we were told. some scholars read local sighting into it; others still hold one sighting can bind everyone who hears of it.

original.note: Arabic: the new crescent moon that begins a month.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone starts Ramadan on the same day.
what it means: communities start the month by local sighting, another country's sighting, or calculation, so dates can differ.
what a scholar hears: 'fast when you see it' in al-Bukhari, the report of Kurayb in Sahih Muslim, and the debate over ikhtilaf al-matali', differing horizons.

notes: Editor: hook's 'it isn't anyone being careless / honest answers' and teach's 'isn't a failure' cut, which repeated the 'nobody is wrong' framing of the days before.
Bukhari 1909: confirm number; the report specifies completing Sha'ban as thirty days; the script says 'complete the month as thirty days'.
Muslim 1087: confirm number and details (Friday night in Syria, Saturday night in Medina).
Positions: local sighting (differing horizons), one sighting binding all who hear, and calculation (either replacing or vetting sightings): confirm fair summary.
'Some councils announce the dates far in advance' (e.g. bodies in North America and Europe using calculation): not named deliberately; confirm.
